label: TMUA 2022 · Paper 1 · Question 18

hints.title: Turn intersections into zeros
hints.body: Consider the difference h(x)=f(x)−g(x). Its degree gives an upper bound on the number of distinct intersections the two graphs can have.
hints.recap: Counting intersections is equivalent to counting zeros of a difference.
hints.pitfall: Repeated factors do not by themselves give different intersection points.
hints.pause: Determine the degree and end behaviour of the difference polynomial.

recall.reminder: Opposite polynomial signs guarantee a root between two inputs; a nonzero polynomial cannot have more distinct roots than its degree.

hints.title: Sample where one expression vanishes
hints.body: Evaluate the sign of h at the zeros of f and at q,r, where g vanishes. Use the positivity of p and the signs of the factored expressions.
hints.recap: At a zero of one function, the difference is controlled by the other function alone.
hints.pitfall: A squared factor is nonnegative, but the remaining unsquared factor can change the sign.
hints.pause: Make a sign table for these sample inputs under each offered ordering.

recall.reminder: A factored polynomial is easiest to analyse by the signs and zeros of its individual factors.

hints.title: Count separate guaranteed crossings
hints.body: For each proposed ordering, arrange the sample inputs on a number line. Every interval whose endpoint signs are opposite contains at least one zero. Include the information from the left-hand tail.
hints.recap: Disjoint sign-change intervals guarantee distinct roots independently of the precise curve heights.
hints.pitfall: A sketch for one chosen scale does not establish a claim for every positive scale.
hints.pause: Find which offered ordering guarantees the degree-limit count for every positive scale, and justify the separate intervals.

recall.reminder: Use the leading term for polynomial tail behaviour and opposite signs to establish roots in disjoint intervals.

solution:
Put h(x)=f(x)−g(x). The difference is

h(x)=x2(x−1)2(x−2)+p(x−q)2(x−r)2

It is a degree-five polynomial, so it has at most five distinct real zeros.

Under option B, 0<q<1<r<2. For every p>0, h(0)>0, h(1)>0, and h(2)>0. But h(q)=f(q)<0 and h(r)=f(r)<0, because these inputs lie below 2 and are not zeros of f. Also h(x)→−∞ as x→−∞.

Continuity therefore gives a zero in each of (−∞,0), (0,q), (q,1), (1,r), and (r,2). These intervals are disjoint, so the zeros are distinct. The degree bound shows that there are exactly five, for every positive p. This is the greatest possible number, so answer B is the offered set that guarantees it.
knowledgePattern: Use alternating signs at polynomial zeros to guarantee distinct crossings
